messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Lukas is a 21-year-old public defender who came to treatment after months of feeling as if danger could arrive at any moment, even in rooms that other people experienced as ordinary. He was born in Europe and came to the United States as a refugee after a violent displacement in late adolescence, an experience he still describes less as a story than as flashes of what he saw. When he speaks about that period at all, it comes in stark visual fragments: a corridor jammed with people trying to move at once, faces turned in panic, the fixed sightline of a doorway that had become an exit and a trap, bodies crouched low and waiting for the next sound. What has stayed with him most vividly are the moments of suspended quiet between bursts of noise, when everyone around him seemed to understand that silence did not mean safety but that something terrible might be about to happen.

In the years since arriving in the U.S., Lukas has built a life that appears unusually accomplished for his age. He is in a relationship and works as a public defender, spending his days in holding areas, crowded courtrooms, and interview rooms where abrupt noises are common and the atmosphere can turn tense without warning. Yet the same environment that makes him good at noticing risk also keeps him in a state of constant alert. A metal door slamming in the courthouse, someone raising a voice in the hall, even a dropped file can make him jolt before he has time to think. He experiences these reactions as immediate and physical, a full-body response that feels as if he is back in the posture he held during the refugee trauma—braced, low, ready for impact. At times there is no picture in his mind at all, only a sudden rush of fear so intense that it feels disproportionate to the moment and yet completely convincing to him.

Lukas has become preoccupied not only with danger around him but with what his own mind is doing. He monitors his thoughts closely for signs that he is losing control or “going crazy,” especially after one of these false alarms. If his heart jumps at a sound or if a wave of terror comes over him in a quiet room, he immediately checks himself: Was that normal? Why did I react like that? Does this mean something is wrong with me? He does not describe elaborate beliefs about the past so much as a settled conviction about the present world. To him, it is simply true that the world is dangerous, that safety is temporary, and that only constant vigilance offers any chance of staying ahead of what might happen next. What frightens him most is not one specific anticipated threat but the sense that danger arrives without warning and that people who relax are the ones who get caught off guard.

Silence is particularly difficult for him. In his office, if the usually noisy corridor suddenly goes still, Lukas feels his body tense before he can identify why. In those moments he is certain something is about to happen. He scans for footsteps, changes in tone, movement at the door. Colleagues may just experience a lull in activity, but for him unusual quiet carries the same shape as the worst moments of his displacement. His memories are often predominantly visual, but not always. Sometimes a client recounting a chaotic scene, or even hearing others mention refugees or aftermaths of war, is enough to bring on the emotional force of the past without any image attached. He feels the terror first and only later realizes that he has drifted into that state again.

Over time Lukas has made his life narrower in ways that feel sensible to him. He avoids talking about what happened, including with his partner, because speaking about it seems likely to pull him back into the same helpless intensity. He also avoids reminders when they come from others. If coworkers begin discussing international conflicts or refugee crises, he finds a reason to leave. If a client’s history overlaps too closely with his own, he keeps the conversation strictly legal and impersonal. This has begun to affect his work; he is still committed and effective, but there are interviews he rushes through, conversations he redirects, and moments when he appears distant just when clients are asking for human connection. At home, his partner has noticed that Lukas goes quiet when certain topics come up and that he is hard to reach emotionally after a day filled with abrupt noises and constant scanning.

What finally brought him in was not a single new event but the accumulation of these moments until they felt inescapable. He recently startled so violently at an ordinary sound in the courthouse that he felt embarrassed in front of colleagues, and afterward he spent hours monitoring his own thoughts, trying to determine whether he was becoming unstable. He is seeking help now because he is exhausted by always being on guard and because he does not want his relationship or his work to shrink further around what he cannot bear to hear or say. At the same time, he is afraid that if he lets his guard down—even in therapy—something terrible will happen, or that speaking plainly about the past will bring it back with full force. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget, but to stop living as though the next danger is already at the door.
